extracted.subtask_description: Rules, theorems, and algorithms for recognizing, parsing, and uniquely decomposing well-formed formulas (wffs), and for proving/using induction and recursion on sets generated by formula-building operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 13A: Balanced parentheses in wffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff has the same number of left as right parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact (established earlier in Section 1.1) is used to argue about the presence of balanced subexpressions when parsing formulas; it underlies the scanning step of the parsing algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 13B: Proper initial segments are left-heavy
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proper initial segment of a wff contains an excess of left parentheses. Thus no proper initial segment of a wff can itself be a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on the family of wffs. The lemma ensures that once a prefix of a wff is parenthesis-balanced it must be a complete constituent (used to force unique choices in parsing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing algorithm for wffs (top-down tree construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step procedure that, given an expression, determines whether it is a legal wff and, if so, constructs the tree showing how it was built from sentence symbols via formula-building operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) If all minimal vertices have sentence symbols, accept; otherwise pick a minimal non-sentence vertex. (2) First symbol must be '('; if second is negation jump to step 4; else go to step 3. (3) Scan left until you first reach (α) where α is a nonempty expression with balanced parentheses; α is the left constituent, next symbol must be a binary connective (∧,∨,→,↔), the remainder β) must be an expression β plus a right parenthesis; create left/right child vertices with α and β, return to step 1. (4) For (¬ β) create one child with β and return to step 1. Rejection footnotes: if first symbol not '(', or required balanced α cannot be found before end, or remainder does not match required form, reject as non-wff and halt. Correctness notes: the algorithm halts (depth bounded by expression length), the choices are forced by Lemmas 13A/13B, rejection implies non-wff, acceptance yields a valid wff and its unique tree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of parse tree / unique readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each wff has a uniquely determined parsing tree (unique decomposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the parsing algorithm's choices are forced (cannot use shorter or longer α without violating balance/initial-segment lemmas), the algorithm constructs the only possible tree for a given wff. Unique readability ensures there are enough parentheses for unambiguous notation and allows unambiguous extension of truth assignments by working up the tree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection criteria in parsing (footnote rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific failure modes in the parsing algorithm cause rejection: if the first symbol is not '(', if the scanner fails to find a balanced left constituent α before the end, or if expected forms (e.g., connective followed by β) are not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions occur the algorithm halts and correctly rejects the expression as non-wff because 'the only possible attempt to make its tree failed.' These explicit rejection rules guarantee soundness of the parser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish (prefix) notation as unambiguous alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish notation (e.g., writing ∧αβ for (α ∧ β)) removes ambiguity and parentheses by prefixing connectives to their arguments; define P-wffs by operations D¬(α)=¬α, D∧(α,β)=∧αβ, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish notation is tidy and well-suited to automatic processing (compilers often convert formulas into Polish notation). Unique readability for such expressions requires a different algorithm; the text promises a unique readability theorem for Polish notation in Section 2.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions for omitting parentheses in ordinary notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Four conventions to write wffs more compactly by omitting some parentheses: (1) outermost parentheses may be omitted (A ∧ B refers to (A ∧ B)); (2) negation applies to as little as possible (¬ A ∧ B means (¬A) ∧ B); (3) conjunction/disjunction apply to as little as possible, respecting (2) (example given for A ∧ B → ¬C ∨ D); (4) repeated connective symbols group to the right (α ∧ β ∧ γ means α ∧ (β ∧ γ), α → β → γ means α → (β → γ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conventions violate earlier strict naming rules but are acceptable because the discussion now restricts attention to expressions that are already wffs. Examples and caveats are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-down and bottom-up definitions of generated sets (C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two equivalent definitions of the set C generated from initial set B by operations f and g: (top-down) C is the intersection of all inductive subsets S ⊇ B closed under f and g; (bottom-up) C is the set of elements reachable by finite construction sequences from B (define Cn as elements obtainable in ≤ n steps and C = ⋃n Cn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction sequences are finite sequences where each element is either in B or results from earlier elements via f or g. Equivalence of the two views is shown; examples include natural numbers, integers, algebraic functions, and wffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction principle for generated sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is generated from B by functions in F, and S ⊆ C includes B and is closed under the functions in F, then S = C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard structural induction principle: to prove a property for all elements of C, show it holds for B and is preserved by the generating operations. Numerous variants (induction on length, number of connective occurrences, etc.) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and criterion for freeness (freely generated sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: C is freely generated from B by f and g iff (1) the restrictions fC and gC are one-to-one, and (2) ranges of fC and gC and the set B are pairwise disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeness rules out collisions like f(x,y)=g(z) or elements of B appearing as results of the operations. Freeness is the key combinatorial condition ensuring recursion/extension theorems hold (avoids contradictory demands on recursively-defined functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion theorem (existence and uniqueness of extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is freely generated from B by operations f and g, and given any target set V with operations F:V×V→V and G:V→V and a map h:B→V, then there is a unique function h:C→V such that h(b)=given h(b) for b∈B, h(f(x,y))=F(h(x),h(y)), and h(g(x))=G(h(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: consider acceptable partial functions satisfying the required equations, take union of all acceptable functions; freeness ensures domain closure and uniqueness. Chromatic analogy: color base elements, combine colors by F/G to color composite elements. Examples: extending truth assignments to all wffs, length counting function, and maps on natural numbers via successor. Warning: if generation is not free, such an extension may not exist (counterexamples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique Readability Theorem for formula-building operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The five formula-building operations (E¬, E∧, E∨, E→, E↔), when restricted to the set of wffs, have ranges disjoint from each other and from the sentence symbols, and are one-to-one; equivalently, the set of wffs is freely generated from the sentence symbols by these five operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: equality of composite wffs (e.g., (α ∧ β) = (γ ∧ δ)) forces α=γ and β=δ by Lemmas 13A/13B (otherwise a balanced proper initial segment would exist), and mismatch of connective symbols yields contradictions, establishing disjoint ranges. This result underpins the recursion theorem application to truth assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping wffs to Boolean functions and semantic characterizations (Theorem 15A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate to each wff α (with sentence symbols among A1,...,An) an n-place Boolean function Bα that maps truth-value n-tuples to the truth value of α. Then (a) α |= β iff for all X∈{F,T}^n, Bα(X) ≤ Bβ(X) (with F<T); (b) α is tautologically equivalent to β iff Bα = Bβ; (c) α is a tautology iff Bα is the constant T function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide truth-table style reasoning; example table for A1 ∧ A2 is given. This identification allows working at the level of Boolean functions rather than syntactic formulas when discussing entailment, equivalence, and tautologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressibility of arbitrary Boolean functions by wffs (Theorem 15B / Post)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n-place Boolean function G (n≥1), there exists a wff α that realizes G (i.e., Bα = G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct α in disjunctive normal form: list all n-tuples X_i where G(X_i)=T, for each such tuple form γ_i as conjunctions of either Aj or ¬Aj depending on truth value in the tuple, and let α be the disjunction γ1 ∨ ... ∨ γk. Examples and handling of the constant-F case (A1 ∧ ¬A1) are given.
